Rules: Each prerequisite pair [a, b] indicates that course b must be taken before course a. Determine if the dependency graph contains any cycles.

data.approach: Cycle Detection in Directed Graph using Depth-First Search (DFS)
data.key_insight: We can model the courses and prerequisites as a directed graph where an edge from `b` to `a` means `b` must be taken before `a`. To determine if all courses can be finished, we must check if the graph contains any cycles. We can use DFS with a recursion stack tracking state (unvisited, visiting, visited) to detect cycles efficiently.

steps.title: Build Adjacency List
steps.detail: Construct an adjacency list to represent the directed graph from the given prerequisite pairs.

steps.title: Track Visit States
steps.detail: Use a state array (or set) to keep track of nodes. 0 means unvisited, 1 means currently visiting (in the current recursion stack), and 2 means fully visited.

steps.title: DFS Traversal for Cycle Detection
steps.detail: For each course, if it is unvisited, perform a DFS. If we encounter a node that is currently in the 'visiting' state, we have found a cycle and return False.

steps.title: Complete Check
steps.detail: If all courses are checked without encountering any cycles, return True.

events.detail: Pattern: Cycle Detection in Directed Graph · 3 hints

data.pattern_summary: This pattern is used to identify loops in directed relationships, which helps determine if a sequence with dependencies can be completed.

pattern_options.name: Cycle Detection in Directed Graph
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The problem asks us to find circular dependencies, which means detecting a cycle in a directed graph.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers work when scanning sorted linear sequences, not when traversing arbitrary dependencies in a graph.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding window is for contiguous sublists or subarrays, not for discrete dependency pairs.

pattern_options.name: Greedy approach
pattern_options.feedback: A greedy choice does not solve graph connectivity and reachability issues reliably.

signals.hint: Implies that following a chain of dependencies might lead you back to a starting point.
Directly points to graph traversal and cycle detection algorithms.
Defines directed edges between items, establishing the graph structure.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach builds an adjacency list from the prerequisites and uses a stack-based traversal starting from each course to explore all paths and check if any path leads back to the starting course.
data.brute_force_why: For each of the V vertices, we perform a traversal that visits up to V vertices and E edges, re-exploring paths multiple times.
data.bottleneck: The algorithm restarts the DFS search from every single node without remembering which nodes or subgraphs have already been fully checked or confirmed cycle-free.
bottleneck_hints: Look at where the traversal restarts for each node.
Notice how much path information is re-evaluated across different starting nodes.
Consider what happens when you traverse a node that you already checked previously.

data.overview: The Course Schedule algorithm determines if all courses can be completed by checking for cycles in a directed prerequisite graph. It uses Depth-First Search with three node states (unvisited, visiting, visited) to safely detect any circular dependencies.
data.intuition: Imagine checking a chain of paperwork approvals; if you ever encounter an office you are currently waiting on, you have hit a circular bottleneck.

pitfalls: Using only a visited boolean array instead of a 3-state array, which leads to false cycle positives on valid shared prerequisites in DAGs.
Forgetting to check all nodes, as disconnected components of the graph will be missed if you only start DFS from node 0.
Incorrectly building the adjacency list direction (confusing prerequisites with dependent courses).

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized solution removes the bottleneck of redundant path exploration by tracking the exact traversal state of each node using a three-state array (0 for unvisited, 1 for visiting, 2 for fully visited). Instead of copying path sets or testing every permutation, it visits each vertex and edge at most once, immediately detecting a cycle if it encounters a node currently in the 'visiting' state.

derivation.note: Allocates the adjacency list array for V vertices.
Iterates through all prerequisite pairs to populate the graph.
Initializes the state array of size V.
Checks if the current node is part of the active path.
Marks the node as currently visiting.
Iterates over all outgoing edges from the current node.
Marks the node as fully processed once all neighbors are explored.
Loops through all courses to ensure disconnected components are visited.

data.time_summary: Building the graph takes O(V + E) time. The DFS traversal visits each vertex once (O(V)) and traverses each directed edge once (O(E)) because the state array prevents re-exploring nodes. Total time complexity is O(V + E).
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(V + E) due to storing the adjacency list (V lists holding E elements total), the recursion stack, and the state array of size V.
data.takeaway: When detecting cycles in a directed graph, use Depth-First Search with a three-state visitation array to track active paths and avoid redundant traversals.
mistakes: Using a simple visited boolean array instead of a three-state array, which incorrectly flags valid diamond dependencies as cycles.
Forgetting to check disconnected components by failing to iterate through all nodes as potential DFS start points.
Modifying or copying sets on every recursion level, which destroys the O(V + E) time efficiency.
